dossier.audience_name: A Dutch or EU public-sector web team told its site may not load Google before consent, and that a public body cannot use a cookie wall
dossier.orientation: Simple Analytics is a website-statistics product that, per its own documentation, runs without cookies, personal data or on-device storage and stores the data it collects in the EU, offered here as a candidate replacement for the Google Analytics loaded on a public body's site before consent.

setup_conditions: If the public body's DPO insists on a signed DPA, the organization must supply its own DPA document for Simple Analytics to review and sign; no standard pre-drafted Simple Analytics DPA is documented (R5, R6).
unverified_requirements: A standard, pre-signed Simple Analytics DPA for buyers whose DPO process requires one before approval is not established; only a case-by-case review-and-sign of a customer-supplied document is documented (R5, R6).
A completed independent security certification (e.g. SOC 2 Type II), which some formal procurement or audit checklists expect, is not established; the status is still 'in progress' (R1, R7, E106).

The vendor's general statement that this makes it 'compliant with all major privacy laws out of the box' (E129) does not name the laws covered, so it cannot by itself answer a specific FG/AVG audit checklist item.
decision_gaps: Is there a published target date for completing the SOC 2 Type II audit, which would change whether DPOs that require a completed certification can proceed now or must wait? (R1, R7)

Does Simple Analytics offer any model/template DPA, or only review customer-drafted agreements, which would change how much legal drafting the public body's own team must do before DPO sign-off? (R5, R6)

What exactly is sent to the non-EU provider when the optional AI assistant is enabled, and is it on by default — this would change whether the EU-hosting claim holds unconditionally for the statistics product itself or only for the core, non-AI feature set? (E79)
defining_need_fit.caveat: Core no-personal-data / no-consent / EU-hosting mechanisms are strongly and consistently documented, but formal DPO sign-off rests on a conditional, customer-supplied DPA review rather than a standard artifact, and SOC 2 Type II remains in progress rather than completed.
defining_need_fit.why: The defining need's architecture (no personal data, no device storage, EU hosting, no consent required) is supported by multiple strong official-documentation facts that hold together as one coherent mechanism; the DPO-review and certification-based parts of the workflow rest on a documented but conditional process and an unfinished certification, which are real secondary gaps rather than a failure of the core claim.

ranked_relevance.why: Directly licenses the 'run without consent' core of the defining need: no cookies or trackers means no visitor consent is required.
Directly licenses the 'process no personal data' core of the defining need and states the no-fingerprinting mechanism behind it.
Directly licenses the 'hosted in the EU' core of the defining need, naming the Netherlands as primary infrastructure.
States the specific mechanism behind 'stores nothing on the device': no cookies, localStorage, or similar browser storage.
States a concrete mechanism behind the no-personal-data claim relevant to surviving a regulator/journalist scan: no IP collection or storage.
States a further mechanism relevant to audit survival: no visitor IDs, profiles, or cross-site identifiers, which a scan would otherwise flag.

Documents the mechanism available for the DPO-review component of the workflow: a review-and-sign process for a customer-supplied DPA, with the stated condition that it must align with the service's no-personal-data architecture.

True and licensed, but a poor fact to lead with for this audience: it confirms SOC 2 Type II is still in progress, not completed, which is better used to answer an objection honestly than to open a pitch.

problem_fits.caveat: P1 bundles multiple Big Tech services (Analytics, Fonts, YouTube) loaded before consent; the licensed evidence addresses replacing the analytics tracker's no-consent-required operation, not Fonts or YouTube embeds elsewhere on the site.
problem_fits.why: The product's documented no-cookie, no-personal-data, no-device-storage mechanism directly removes the specific before-consent Google Analytics load the problem describes, but the problem statement's other named services are outside what this evidence covers.
